group.passage:
For well over a thousand years, doctors in Europe learned about blood from the writings of Galen, a Greek physician born in AD 129. In his view, the liver turned the food we eat into blood, which then flowed out through the veins to the rest of the body and was used up there as nourishment. New blood therefore had to be made all the time.
William Harvey, an English doctor who had trained in Italy, decided to test this idea with simple arithmetic. In a book published in 1628, he estimated that the heart could hold about two ounces of blood and supposed that each beat pushed out only a small part of it, perhaps as little as an eighth. Even with such cautious numbers, the result was startling. Since the heart beats more than 1,000 times in half an hour, it would send more blood into the arteries in that short time than the whole body contains. Harvey added that even if the same amount took a whole day to pass through the heart, no amount of food could make up for it. The liver could not possibly keep up. The only answer, he argued, was that the same blood travels around the body again and again.
He backed up his numbers with a simple test. After tying a band tightly around a person’s upper arm, which made the veins of the forearm swell, he pressed on one of them. Blood could easily be pushed along the vein toward the heart, but it would not move the other way, because small valves inside the vein blocked it.
Harvey’s book was short, and it was not welcomed. Critics attacked it, and fewer patients came to see him. Part of the problem was a gap he could not fill: he could not show how blood got from the arteries into the veins. That missing link was found by the Italian scientist Marcello Malpighi, who used a microscope to study the lungs of a frog and saw tiny vessels connecting the two. His findings appeared in 1661, four years after Harvey’s death. Even so, by the time Harvey died, his idea had already begun to win supporters.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention that the same amount of blood might take a whole day to pass through the heart?

options.A: To point out a mistake in Harvey’s arithmetic.
options.B: To show that Harvey’s argument held up even with far slower figures.
options.C: To explain why Galen thought the body needed new blood every day.
options.D: To suggest that Harvey did not know how fast the heart really beats.

questions.stem: Based on Harvey’s reasoning, which finding would have given the most support to Galen’s view?

options.A: The heart holds far more than two ounces of blood.
options.B: The heart beats more than 1,000 times in half an hour.
options.C: Blood in the veins moves only toward the heart.
options.D: Each beat of the heart pushes out almost no blood at all.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true according to the passage?

options.A: Harvey used a microscope to find the vessels that link arteries and veins.
options.B: Most doctors accepted Harvey’s ideas as soon as his book appeared.
options.C: Evidence showing how blood gets from arteries to veins appeared only after Harvey’s death.
options.D: Galen believed that the heart made new blood all the time.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes how the passage is organized?

options.A: An old belief is described, a challenge to it is explained, and a final piece of proof is added.
options.B: Two doctors’ opposite views are compared point by point.
options.C: Harvey’s life is traced from his training in Italy to his death.
options.D: A problem is described, and several possible solutions are weighed.

1.strategy_zh: 目的題要問「作者為什麼放這句」：看它前後的論證。先算出驚人的結果，再說「就算慢很多也一樣」，是在強化結論、排除反駁。
hints: 哈維一開始用的數字是偏大還是偏小？
「一整天」比「半小時」慢了多少？結論有沒有改變？
這句話是在幫哈維的論證加分，還是在挑他的毛病？

2.explanation_zh: 哈維的論證是：心臟每次送出的血量 × 跳動次數，遠超過肝臟能從食物造出的血，所以血必須循環。如果心臟每跳一次幾乎沒有送出血，總量就很小，肝臟就可能跟得上，蓋倫「血由肝臟製造、在身體各處用掉」的說法就站得住，所以選 D。

option_notes_zh.B: 心跳超過 1,000 次正是哈維自己論證的前提，會讓總量更大，支持的是哈維。
option_notes_zh.C: 靜脈的血只往心臟流，是哈維綁手臂實驗的結果，支持的是血液循環。

2.strategy_zh: 機制推論題先把論證拆成「前提 → 結論」：哈維的結論靠的是「每次送出的血量」和「跳動次數」相乘很大。要支持相反的說法，就要找能讓這個乘積變小的發現。

3.explanation_zh: 最後一段說哈維無法說明血如何從動脈進入靜脈，這個缺口後來由馬爾皮吉用顯微鏡看到連接兩者的微小血管才補上，而他的發現在 1661 年發表，是哈維死後四年。所以說明血液如何從動脈流到靜脈的證據，是在哈維過世之後才發表的，選 C。

3.strategy_zh: 是非題要逐一核對人物、時間與器官：把「誰用顯微鏡」「何時發現」「哪個器官造血」對回原文。「死後四年」是時間的線索，要和題目選項的「之後」對上。

4.explanation_zh: 第一段介紹蓋倫的舊說法（肝臟造血、血在身體用掉）；第二、三段說明哈維用計算與綁手臂的實驗挑戰這個說法；最後一段說哈維留下的缺口（動脈如何連到靜脈）由馬爾皮吉補上。這正是「舊觀念 → 提出挑戰 → 補上最後的證據」，所以選 A。
evidence: For well over a thousand years, doctors in Europe learned about blood from the writings of Galen, a Greek physician born in AD 129.

option_notes_zh.C: 以偏概全：文中只提到哈維在義大利受訓與他的死，大部分篇幅在談他的論證，並不是生平傳記。
option_notes_zh.D: 文中沒有提出好幾個解決方法來比較。

translation_zh.text:
一千多年來，歐洲的醫生都從蓋倫的著作學習血液的知識；蓋倫是西元 129 年出生的希臘醫師。他認為，肝臟把我們吃下的食物變成血，血再經由靜脈流到身體各處，在那裡被當作養分用掉。因此，身體必須不斷製造新的血。
曾在義大利受訓的英國醫生威廉‧哈維決定用簡單的算術來檢驗這個想法。在 1628 年出版的一本書中，他估計心臟大約可以裝兩盎司的血，並假設每跳一次只送出其中一小部分，也許少到只有八分之一。即使用這麼保守的數字，結果仍然驚人。心臟半小時內會跳超過 1,000 次，因此在這麼短的時間內送進動脈的血，就會比全身所有的血還多。哈維還補充說，就算同樣的血量要花一整天才流過心臟，吃再多食物也補不回來。肝臟不可能跟得上。他主張，唯一的解釋就是同樣的血一次又一次地在身體裡循環。
他用一個簡單的實驗來支持他的數字。他用帶子把一個人的上臂緊緊綁住，讓前臂的靜脈鼓起來，然後按壓其中一條。血可以輕易地沿著靜脈推向心臟，卻無法往反方向移動，因為靜脈裡的小瓣膜會把它擋住。
哈維的書篇幅不長，而且並不受歡迎。批評者攻擊它，來找他看病的人也變少了。問題之一在於他無法填補的一個缺口：他無法說明血如何從動脈進入靜脈。這個缺少的環節後來由義大利科學家馬爾皮吉找到；他用顯微鏡觀察青蛙的肺，看到連接兩者的微小血管。他的發現在 1661 年發表，是哈維死後四年。儘管如此，在哈維過世時，他的想法已經開始贏得支持者。

open_tasks.prompt: Harvey used small, cautious numbers in his calculation. In 1–2 English sentences, explain why this made his argument stronger rather than weaker.
reference_answers: If even very small numbers show that the heart moves more blood than the body holds, then the real, larger numbers make the point even more clearly.
Using cautious numbers meant critics could not say he had exaggerated, so his conclusion that blood circulates was harder to reject.
checklist_zh: 有沒有說出「保守的數字算出來都已經超過，真實數字只會更多」
有沒有提到這樣能讓批評者難以反駁
是否用自己的話說明，而不是照抄原文
